extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/logic (interested in metaphysics and the theory of predication)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic account of what can be named or predicated: classification of Things (Feelings, Substances, Attributes) and criteria for defining qualities, quantities, and relations in terms of sensations and states of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic limit: know only sensations and their order
rubrics_metrics.description: All we know of objects is the sensations which they give us, and the order of the occurrence of those sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly affirms (with reference to Berkeley, Kant, Cousin, and Sir William Hamilton) that representation—'the matter of which consists of our sensations'—is all we know of an object; the real nature of the Thing in itself remains 'an impenetrable mystery'. Use this principle as the starting epistemic constraint when defining or ascribing properties to external objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Body (substratum/matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A body is conceived as the unknown external cause (a 'substratum') to which we refer sensations; matter is the name commonly given to this substratum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes skeptics' objections (annihilation thought-experiment) and that existence of matter cannot be proved by extrinsic evidence; the common reply is that belief in matter is intuitive. When attributing bodily existence, treat it as an inferred unknown cause adequate to produce sensations rather than as directly knowable substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Mind is the unknown recipient or percipient of feelings; what we know of mind is only the series of its states of consciousness (sensations, thoughts, emotions, volitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like body, mind is only known via its states (a 'thread of consciousness' per James Mill). One may name 'myself' as distinct from the series of states, but no additional knowledge of its inmost nature is claimed or possible within these limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes classified into Quality, Quantity, Relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes are usually distributed under the three heads of Quality, Quantity, and Relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy structures further analysis: treat any attribute as fitting one of these three categories; subsequent criteria explain what grounds each category in experience or consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality grounded on sensation (foundation concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quality (e.g., whiteness) is grounded on the sensation produced in us by the object; the sensation is the 'foundation' of the quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives the whiteness example: ascribing a quality amounts to asserting that the object excites a particular sensation. It allows two interpretive views—quality as identical with sensation, or quality as a power in the object—but for logical purposes adopts language compatible with either and treats sensation as the essential provable element. Avoid invoking occult 'powers' when the sensation suffices as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality as power to excite sensation (paraphrase of ascription)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we say an object 'has' a quality, we assert it possesses the power (capacity) to excite the corresponding sensation in us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formulation 'quality = power to excite sensations' is recommended as a usable logical definition. The account warns against explaining the production of sensations by positing additional occult causes (Molière example) and treats such formulations as mere restatements rather than explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation: fundamentum relationis (fact/phenomenon involving both parties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation between two things is grounded on some fact or phenomenon into which both things enter as parties concerned—the 'fundamentum relationis'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: greater/less (inclusion potential), master/servant (services undertaken). To ascribe a relation, identify the joint fact or series of facts (often describable in terms of states of consciousness) that grounds the relative names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations grounded in states of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Most relations (especially complex ones like legal relations) are grounded on states of consciousness—thoughts, feelings, volitions, intentions, and acts—either of the related minds or of others (e.g., a judge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat external objects as causes that excite those states, but analyze relations in terms of the mental states and relevant intentions/acts that constitute the fundamentum. This is especially pertinent for social/legal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple relations (succession, simultaneity) are states of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Succession and simultaneity (and likewise likeness/unlikeness) are peculiar relations that are either involved in the sensations themselves or are feelings (states of consciousness) of succession or resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These simple relations do not admit of the same sort of external-fact analysis as other relations; our knowledge and possibility of knowledge of them is confined to their manifestation among sensations or states of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likeness/unlikeness as feelings of resemblance; ambiguity with identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Resemblance is a feeling (a state of the observer's consciousness); complex resemblances resolve into resemblances of parts and of arrangement. The word 'same' is ambiguous between identity and undistinguishable resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming likeness, specify whether you mean strict identity or high similarity; analyze complex likeness by decomposing it into simpler likenesses between constituent parts and their arrangement (examples: portrait, mimicry, analogy between historic relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity grounded in differences of sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in quantity (e.g., a gallon vs ten gallons) are grounded on measurable differences in the sensations they produce; quantity is a kind of likeness/unlikeness in the sensations excited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account emphasizes that while we can assert that sensations differ with quantity, we cannot further explain what the sensation 'is'—we must accept the difference as a part of the constitution of things. Use sensory-difference evidence as the basis for quantity-claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of minds include internal states and effects on other minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes ascribed to minds may be grounded either in the mind's own states (habits of feeling) or in the feelings they excite in other minds; sometimes both are predicated (e.g., 'generous' implies a state and that it excites approbation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ascribing moral or evaluative attributes, make explicit the twofold claim: (1) recurring states in the subject's sentient life, and (2) the sentiment (approval/disapproval) such states excite in observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: General taxonomy of Namable Things (summary criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Namable things fall into: Feelings (sensations, thoughts, emotions, volitions), Substances (bodies as unknown causes; minds as unknown recipients), and Attributes (Quality, Relation, Quantity), each ultimately known via sensations or states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite framework to structure logical analysis or classification: begin with identifying feelings, then infer substances only as unknown causes/recipients, and finally analyze attributes by grounding them in sensations or in facts composed of sensations/states of consciousness.
